name: Joanne Robertson
label: AD 93
lede: A painter who has been singing since childhood, a voice on Dean Blunt's darkest records, and, in 2025, a No. 8 album of the year on Pitchfork, made between painting sessions while raising a child.

eras.title: Christmas Day debut
eras.text: Robertson trained as a painter and started putting out records at the same time. Her first album arrived on a small label on December 25, 2007.

years.h: The Lighter comes out on Textile Records
years.p: Robertson's debut album is minimal and homemade, and it lands on Christmas Day 2007. One reviewer later heard the stripped-down approach of her 2020 EP already in it.
years.xp:
Wikipedia dates the release to December 25, 2007 on Textile Records, while a 2020 review of her later EP places The Lighter in 2008. Either way, it is the start of a discography that runs on private, diary-like records rather than campaigns.

By then she was also a working painter: she studied painting at Glasgow School of Art and took an MFA at the Slade, and by her mid-twenties was already showing at the ICA in London, according to Antenne Books.

eras.title: The voice on Dean Blunt's records
eras.text: Robertson's breakout audience came sideways: as the vocalist on two albums by Dean Blunt, the London artist formerly of Hype Williams.

years.h: She sings "Demon" and "Imperial Gold" on Dean Blunt's The Redeemer
years.p: Robertson takes vocals on two tracks of Blunt's second solo album, out on Hippos in Tanks and World Music.
years.xp:
Wikipedia credits Robertson with vocals on "Demon" and "Imperial Gold". Vice's Colin Joyce wrote that the album "sounds how a breakup feels", and Fact ranked it No. 1 on its 50 best albums of 2013.

It set up a long working relationship: Blunt would become the collaborator she is most often named beside.

years.h: Back on Blunt's Black Metal, now on Rough Trade
years.p: Robertson is a frequent vocalist on Blunt's Black Metal, released November 3, 2014 via Rough Trade. Tiny Mix Tapes and Crack both called it 2014's best album.
years.xp: Wikipedia names Robertson as a collaborator and vocalist on the album, which Metacritic scores 79. The Observer's Killian Fox wrote that it held "some of the most achingly beautiful music recorded this year."

eras.title: Her own records, from Glasgow
eras.text: Robertson released albums under her own name, made a record with Blunt, published poems and settled in Glasgow.

years.p: Released June 22, 2016 on Escho, it takes a notably different stylistic direction from her collaborations, per one 2020 reviewer.

years.h: Wahalla: a full album with Dean Blunt
years.p: Wikipedia lists the record as a collaboration with Dean Blunt on World Music and Textile Records, released May 8, 2017. Test Pressing later described it as experimental, trip-hop territory.

years.h: A book of poems about 1971 with Byron Coley, and a move to Glasgow
years.p: Robertson and the American writer Byron Coley publish 1971 (A Year in Record Reviews Poems), and she relocates from London to Glasgow.
years.xp:
Antenne Books says she co-founded Bad Taste Press with Coley, publishing experimental books that cross mediums. Cafe OTO's biography says she moved to Glasgow in 2018, having been based in London.

In the same year she made the painting Stupid Girls, the image that gave her 2020 record its title, according to Wikipedia.

years.p: Six pieces of folk-leaning guitar and voice, opening with "am i grief" and closing with the seven-minute "peacecraft".
years.xp: Test Pressing gave the release date as March 28, 2020, digital only at first. A reviewer at Era Journal called it a maturation of the minimalist approach already audible on The Lighter, and heard the warmth of indie sleaze and shoegaze in the reverb.

eras.title: Collaborator, painter, archivist
eras.text: Robertson moved between rooms: Dean Blunt's Rough Trade albums, an art-world record with Sidsel Meineche Hansen, and a solo album of songs written over a decade.

years.p: Robertson sings on several tracks of [[Dean Blunt|e8bd5b47-e8b4-4671-a9f6-590a92e88898]]'s Rough Trade album, which Pitchfork scored 8.1.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists her vocals on tracks including "Vigil", "Dash Snow", "Sketamine" and "The Rot". The album holds a Metacritic score of 84 and reached the top 10 of several 2021 lists, including No. 3 at The Quietus.

years.h: Alien Baby 0 Rules for Life, with the sculptor Sidsel Meineche Hansen
years.p: Tenderbooks puts out a 12-inch of Robertson and the artist Sidsel Meineche Hansen, edition of 250, backed by Arts Council England.
years.xp: Tenderbooks says the pair had already worked together on a 2020 video project with the writer Reba Maybury. The Wire's introduction to Robertson describes the record as a concept album exploring a reciprocal sense of humour around being a woman.

years.h: Blue Car, songs written over about ten years, on AD 93
years.p: Her first record for AD 93 gathers solo recordings whose original dates even she can't pin down.
years.xp: Cafe OTO's biography says the tracks were written over roughly ten years, with original recording dates unknown. It describes her releases as working like diary entries, snapshots from specific points in time.

years.p: Robertson's fifth album, released May 27, 2024 on World Music, the same imprint as [[Dean Blunt|e8bd5b47-e8b4-4671-a9f6-590a92e88898]]'s The Redeemer. That October she also guests on [[Elias Rønnenfelt|f2874ad8-a75d-4388-b5b9-0724c79e7eda]]'s Heavy Glory.

eras.title: Blurrr
eras.text: After nearly twenty years of releases, the record that gets her on a year-end list arrives, made in the gaps of a busy life.

years.h: "Gown" opens the campaign, with a cello
years.p: The first single, "Gown", pairs Robertson's voice with strings by [[Oliver Coates|c464a09c-6e10-469b-82a1-0234b189790c]]; "Always Were" follows August 27.
years.xp: Stereogum's Chris DeVille heard a certain ineffable grace in her delivery, and pointed out that Coates has scored Aftersun and played on Radiohead's A Moon Shaped Pool. A video for "Always Were" also went up on YouTube.

q: I think that's how everyone writes music; they just start playing.
years.src: Album of the Year · Paste · Clash · Wikipedia: Blurrr
yt: Always Were, Joanne Robertson & Oliver Coates
years.h: Blurrr: recorded between painting and raising a kid
years.p: Nine tracks, 43 minutes, co-produced with cellist Oliver Coates, who plays on "Always Were", "Gown" and "Doubt". Pitchfork gave it 9.0 and Best New Music.
years.xp:
Her Bandcamp page says the songs were made "in between painting sessions and also whilst raising a child". Pitchfork's Emma Madden called it Robertson's "undisputed masterpiece" (score 9.0, per Album of the Year), and Paste's Devon Chodzin heard a midpoint between Arthur Russell and Hope Sandoval. Metacritic lists it at 90.

Robertson, who grew up in Blackpool, told Paste improvisation is not a special category for her. Clash gave it 8/10, calling it a muted gem.

years.p: Pitchfork ranks Blurrr No. 8 on its 50 best albums of 2025; TIME puts it No. 6 on its top ten.
years.xp: According to Wikipedia, Blurrr also came first on The Guardian's experimental albums list, and appeared on Crack Magazine's year-end list.
